name: Kasner Anisotropic Vacuum Cosmology
description: An anisotropic vacuum cosmology that expands along some axes while contracting along another, with expansion exponents constrained by two algebraic relations. It is a key building block of the chaotic approach to cosmological singularities.
history: The standard picture of the first instant of the universe was written down by a man with no interest in the universe. Edward Kasner was a geometer at Columbia, and what he wanted from Einstein's field equations was a question of shape: how many flat dimensions does it take to hold a solution inside one as a curved slice? In April 1921 he proved that five will not do [kasner1921flat]. Six months later came the five page paper relativists cite to this day [kasner1921]. Its third section opens with the words "A simple example" and then gives, in a few lines, the metric that now carries his name: three spatial directions going as powers of the time, their exponents obeying two conditions, that they sum to one and that their squares sum to one. What interests Kasner is that such spreads embed in a flat space of seven dimensions. He adds that it "can be put in the static form," which tells you what he thought he had.¶Read the two conditions as geometry and they are a plane and a sphere. The plane $p_1 + p_2 + p_3 = 1$ cuts the unit sphere $p_1^2 + p_2^2 + p_3^2 = 1$ in a circle, and every Kasner universe is one point on it. Apart from three isolated points where the geometry is secretly flat, one exponent comes out negative: sorted, the first lies between $-1/3$ and $0$, the second between $0$ and $2/3$, the third between $2/3$ and $1$. Two axes stretch, the third squeezes, and the squeeze is compulsory. Run it back toward $t = 0$ and the stretching directions crush to nothing while the contracting one runs away, so its singularity is met not as a point but as a cigar, unboundedly long and unboundedly thin.¶Its second life came out of an argument one side lost badly. In 1963 Evgeny Lifshitz and Isaak Khalatnikov took Kasner's exponents as the leading behavior of a region collapsing toward a singularity, then counted the arbitrary functions such a solution can carry, and came up short. A singularity, they concluded, is what special initial data buys you, an artifact of Friedmann's perfect symmetry rather than a verdict of the theory [lifshitz1963]. For most of a decade that was the Soviet position, and it was wrong. Roger Penrose took the premise apart in 1965 by assuming no symmetry whatever: once a trapped surface forms, geodesics end, and generality is no protection [penrose1965].¶What the losing side did next is the part worth telling. Hunting their own error, Lifshitz and Khalatnikov, joined by Vladimir Belinskii, found the regime they had skipped. Near a singularity neighboring points stop speaking to one another, and each one alone sits in a Kasner solution for a while, hands the negative exponent to a different axis, then sits in another [khalatnikov1970, bkl1970]. The axis collapsing this epoch is expanding the next, and the succession runs on one number: parametrize the exponents by $u$, and each bounce sends $u$ to $u - 1$ until it falls below one, whereupon the era closes and the next opens at $1/u$, the map that manufactures continued fractions, so an irrational start never repeats. Charles Misner had found the same oscillation in the closed Bianchi type IX model, named it the Mixmaster universe after the kitchen appliance, and hoped the churning would beat the early universe smooth [misner1969]. It does not churn hard enough. Kasner thought the best thing in his paper was the metric in section four, "apparently the simplest solution of Einstein's equations which has thus far been obtained." That is not the one anybody remembers.
